title: Freud vs Aristotle: Human nature at war with itself
subtitle: Pessimism and the myth of progress
author: Edward Harcourt
introduction: Many have sought to harmonize our human nature with the demands of society. Some philosophers like Aristotle even thought the perfection of our human nature and the demands of civic life went hand in hand. Freud disagreed. Drawing on Freud's persistent pessimism, philosopher Edward Harcourt argues that civilization and our instincts are permanently at odds. Contrary to many forms of contemporary psychoanalytic thought, Harcourt argues that psychoanalysis cannot make this conflict go away. It can only bring it more sharply into view.
body:
Freud and Aristotle aren’t always spoken about in the same breath, but though Freud gets filed under “psychoanalysis” and Aristotle under “philosophy,” they grappled with many of the same questions. So if we want to understand Freud’s pessimism, Aristotle is a good place to start, not because he shared it but because he didn’t.

Aristotle thought our “first nature”—what we’re born with, our biological endowment—is capable of thoroughgoing transformation by culture, education, induction into a society and its ways: what the Germans call Bildung. And the results of that transformation are twofold: first of all, the acquisition of the virtues and, secondly, eudaemonia or happiness. For Aristotle thought not only that we are made for virtue, but also that virtue and happiness go together. The human beings who perfect their natural endowments will not only be happy, but also more or less effortlessly inhabit civic life. Pursuing political ambitions—even pursuing personal fame and greatness—fit into this account, since self-denial doesn’t have the same place in Aristotle’s view of the virtues as it does in later Christian or post-Christian formulations. (“Lack of proper ambition” is an Aristotelian vice.) But such pursuits must be equipped with motivations of truthfulness, justice, kindness, and fidelity to promises—civic virtues—all under the guidance of practical wisdom, so these apparently competing motivations can be navigated without conflict.

In one of [Freud's] most frequently quoted remarks, psychoanalysis replaces neurosis with “ordinary unhappiness”.

That’s an attractive picture because the virtues and self-realization—taking the developmental path that your nature has laid down for you—come together as part of a single package. And with some variations, it’s a picture we also find outside philosophy, in some post-Freudian psychoanalytic thinkers, DW Winnicott, for example. Though he has a broader conception than Aristotle of what Bildung brings with it—art, religion, and play are in there—these are all part of the proper development of our natures, not in tension with it.

Freud rejects this optimistic picture. To be sure, he thinks—not unlike Aristotle—that it’s part of our human natures to shape up for civic life as we develop. In fact, he thinks we need to do so in order merely to survive: if we lived by the pleasure principle alone—hallucinating the objects that satisfy our instincts—we wouldn’t last long. The trouble is that in shaping up for civic life, our “first natures” are not, as in Aristotle or Winnicott, transformed without residue. On the contrary, all sorts of inconvenient and conflicting impulses stick around, creating the possibility for psychic conflict and potentially making mischief all our lives long.

This pessimism is a persistent thread in Freud’s writing, though it takes different forms in different phases of his thinking. In the late “dual instinct” theory, for example, he asks why we comply with the demands of civilization, given that so much in our instinctual endowment pulls us in the opposite direction. His answer is that this is our own aggression restraining itself. But the fact that compliance is explained by an internal mechanism doesn’t make the business conflict-free. On the contrary, the superego—the agent of aggression turned upon ourselves—is stationed in the ego “like the garrison in an occupied city.” The citizens, that is, comply because they are coerced. Their dissident impulses have to find expression elsewhere.

But hang on: isn’t psychoanalysis at least partly about notions like integration, so can’t it make these conflicts go away? According to some of the optimistic post-Freudian versions of psychoanalysis I’ve referred to already, yes, but arguably not according to Freud himself. Freud thinks psychoanalysis can make neurosis go away—that is, symptom-formation as a response to unacknowledged inner conflict. But all that will do is bring the frustrations of civilized living more sharply into view. In one of his most frequently quoted remarks, psychoanalysis replaces neurosis with “ordinary unhappiness.”

Memorably grim as that remark is, though, there are after all some more optimistic strains in Freud, though they don’t in the end get us very far. Alongside the notion of repression, Freud also introduces the notion of sublimation—a psychological mechanism that transforms instincts rather than merely driving them out of view. As he says, though “generally speaking our civilization is built upon the suppression of instincts,” it’s in “the capacity to exchange [the] original … aim” of an instinct—which he thinks is sexual—for another one which “has a higher social or ethical valuation”  that sublimation’s “value for civilization” lies. That sounds rather like Aristotle and “second nature.” Unfortunately, however, it’s not clear how sublimation fits into the rest of Freud’s theory of instinct: though it has “a special quality which we shall one day be able to characterize in metaphysical terms,” that day never actually came about. So that optimistic strain of Freudian thinking remains underdeveloped.

There’s another one too, which it’s easy to overlook, and this is Freud’s sexual liberalism. While some of the psychic costs of civic life are owed to inevitable features of human nature, some—and you don’t need Freudian theory to see the appeal of this idea—are owed to buttoned-up sexual mores local to this or that society. (Local to Freud’s own and—in Freud’s day, at least—still more so to that of the United States.) Liberalize the mores—fewer taboos on extramarital sex for example—and the psychic costs of civic life are immediately lowered because less repression is required to achieve it. But as long as there’s more to our unintegrated impulses than can be addressed by liberalized sexual mores, as there surely is, that idea—like the idea of sublimation—only goes so far in mitigating Freudian pessimism.

SUGGESTED READING Freud was wrong, psychoanalysis is a moral pursuit By Edward Harcourt

Freud’s pessimism so far can all be traced back to the inevitability of frustration. But his conception of the aims of an instinct yields an outlook which, if anything, is more deeply pessimistic still, because it goes to what we would accomplish if our instincts were satisfied. Freud gives two accounts of the “aim” of an instinct: first, that instincts aim at pleasure understood as an experience of some kind, and secondly that they aim at their own extinction—an account we also find in places as diverse as Arthur Schopenhauer and Bertrand Russell. But given that an instinct’s seeking extinction is the “program of the pleasure-principle,” it looks like an instinct’s aim is pleasure. When the reality principle comes on the scene, human beings are supplied with more “objects” than they had before, but the “aim” remains the same: the route to pleasure becomes more circuitous, but everything that’s desired is desired ultimately as a means to it. That seemingly innocent philosophical move has a dramatic effect: anything apparently done for its own sake—from the baby playing at the breast to the creation of a work of art—is in fact done simply as the means to a state of oneself, either “the experiencing of strong feelings of pleasure” or,  if this for Freud is really a distinct answer, the extinction of the painful state of wanting to do it. This view of human purposes yields a pessimistic view of life if our one universal desire is always partially frustrated, but the picture scarcely cheers up if we imagine it fulfilled: all human motivation comes out sounding oddly like addiction. Given his assumptions, Freud is thus quite right to puzzle over why “the crudest, but also the most effective methods of influencing [our own organism],” namely “the chemical one—intoxication,” is not more widely pursued than it is.

A final reflection takes us back to Aristotle. The Aristotelian, integrative picture of human nature has achieved prominence in recent times thanks to the visibility of “virtue ethics.” Now some twentieth and twenty-first century versions of this outlook are Aristotelian in form but unAristotelian in content: virtue goes with the perfection of our natures and with eudaemonia (as Aristotle said), but the catalogue of virtues shrinks to the moral virtues of justice, generosity, fidelity to promises, and so on, thereby echoing a kind of moral mania that seems to be on the rise elsewhere too. Some have described this as a new puritanism.

But how could anyone realize themselves merely by keeping promises and the like—what about fun, friendship, curiosity, ambition? And if we are wise enough, like Aristotle, to keep plenty of “ego” in our list of the virtues which a properly acculturated person would possess, how are all these different traits really supposed to cohabit without conflict? We can’t do without fun, ambition, and the rest, but we all also have an interest in not being lied to and stolen from, so it looks as if we need the moral virtues too. So—even if we don’t follow Freud in locating frustration in the conflict between instinct and the demands of social living—it re-enters the picture by another route: the richer the set of virtues, the greater the opportunity for conflict between them. That creates a significant place for another virtue, taught both by Freud and elsewhere in the psychoanalytic tradition: the capacity to look internal conflict clearly in the eye.
